9350:
Isolated means separated from everything else — cut off, alone, or apart.

Think of a small island in the middle of a vast ocean. Nothing around it. No bridges, no nearby land, no easy way to reach it or leave it. That island is isolated. This single image captures the soul of the word: something (or someone) that has been pulled away from the rest, left standing alone.
The Three Main Ways It's Used

The word "isolated" works in three broad areas of life: people and feelings, places, and events or things.

1. Isolated People (Emotionally or Physically Cut Off)

When a person is isolated, they are cut off from others — either physically (they can't be around people) or emotionally (they feel alone even if people are nearby).

Examples:

  • "After moving to a new city where she knew nobody, she felt completely isolated."
  • "The patient was kept isolated in a hospital room so the infection wouldn't spread to others."
  • "Elderly people who live alone can become isolated if no one visits or calls them."

Notice that isolation can happen from the outside (someone puts you apart — like the patient in a hospital) or from the inside (you feel disconnected, even in a crowd). Both are valid uses.

Key feeling it carries: loneliness, disconnection, being cut off from the flow of normal life.

2. Isolated Places (Remote, Hard to Reach)

When describing a location, isolated means it is far away from other places, people, or communities — difficult to get to, with little or nothing around it.

Examples:

  • "They built a cabin in an isolated valley deep in the mountains."
  • "The village was so isolated that mail was only delivered once a week."
  • "Scientists set up a research station in one of the most isolated parts of Antarctica."

An isolated place is not just "quiet" or "peaceful" — it carries the specific meaning of being geographically cut off or remote. A park in a city is quiet, but it isn't isolated. A farmhouse with no neighbors for 50 miles? That's isolated.

3. Isolated Events or Cases (Occurring Alone, Not Part of a Pattern)

This is a very important and commonly misunderstood use. When we call an event, incident, or case isolated, we mean it is a single, rare occurrence — not part of a larger trend or pattern.

Examples:

  • "Police said the attack was an isolated incident and that the area remains safe."
  • "Doctors found an isolated tumor — just one, with no signs of spreading."
  • "There were a few isolated showers in the afternoon, but most of the day was sunny."

Here, "isolated" is doing a specific job: it's telling you not to generalize. One thing happened. It was unusual. It does not mean it will keep happening or that there is a bigger problem.

This is why politicians, officials, and doctors love the phrase "isolated incident" — it signals: "This was a one-off. Don't read too much into it."

"Isolated" isn't always all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum of intensity, and the word can reflect different degrees.

  • A person can be slightly isolated (they see people less than they'd like) or completely isolated (they have had no human contact for weeks).
  • A place can be relatively isolated (a small town two hours from a city) or deeply isolated (a research post in the middle of the Arctic).
  • An event can be largely isolated (it happened once, with only minor similar cases) or truly isolated (a completely unique, one-time occurrence).

Context and surrounding words (like "very," "completely," "relatively") will help you know where on the spectrum something falls.
The Feeling the Word Carries (Its Tone)

"Isolated" almost always has a slightly negative or serious tone. It suggests something is wrong, difficult, or worth noting:

  • An isolated person is missing connection — we understand that as a hardship.
  • An isolated place is hard to reach or help — there's a sense of vulnerability.
  • An isolated incident is something people often say to calm concern — which itself tells you the situation was concerning enough to require calming.

It is rarely used to describe something positive. You would not normally say "I found a beautifully isolated café" the way you'd say "I found a wonderfully cozy café." Instead, you might say "a secluded café" (secluded carries a softer, more pleasant tone). This distinction matters.
Isolated vs. Words That Look Similar

These words are close in meaning but not identical. Understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding of "isolated."

Isolated vs. Lonely
"Lonely" is a feeling — it's purely emotional. "Isolated" is a condition — a state of being separated, which may or may not lead to loneliness. You can be isolated without feeling lonely (a monk who happily lives alone in the mountains). You can feel lonely without being isolated (in the middle of a busy city, surrounded by strangers).

Isolated vs. Alone
"Alone" simply means no one else is present. It's neutral. "I went for a walk alone." "Isolated" carries the idea of being cut off — there's distance, separation, and often difficulty involved. "She was isolated from her family for months."

Isolated vs. Remote
"Remote" is almost always about physical distance and is commonly used for places or working arrangements (remote work, a remote area). "Isolated" includes physical distance but also extends to emotional disconnection and singular events. All isolated places are remote, but "remote" doesn't always carry the same sense of being cut off or left behind.

Isolated vs. Secluded
"Secluded" often carries a positive or deliberate tone — a secluded beach, a secluded garden. It means private and sheltered, often by choice. "Isolated" is more neutral-to-negative and often implies something unintended or difficult.
Common Collocations (Words That Naturally Travel With "Isolated")

Certain words pair very naturally with "isolated." Learning these combinations will help you recognize and use the word in real life:

  • Isolated incident — a single event, not part of a pattern
  • Isolated community — a group of people living far from the rest of society
  • Isolated area / region — a remote place
  • Isolated case — a single medical or legal case that stands alone
  • Feel isolated — to experience emotional disconnection
  • Become isolated — to gradually lose contact with others
  • Isolated showers — in weather, scattered and infrequent rain in a few spots
  • Isolated system — in science, a system with no interaction with the outside world
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Isolated" means cut off, separated, or standing alone — away from others, from society, or from a pattern.

  • A person is isolated when they are cut off from connection.
  • A place is isolated when it is far from everything else, hard to reach.
  • An event is isolated when it is a rare, single occurrence that doesn't represent a wider trend.

The word carries a tone of disconnection and separation, and it usually signals that something is worth paying attention to — because being isolated, in most contexts, is a condition of hardship, remoteness, or rarity.
9351:
Isolation means the state of being separated from everything else — people, places, groups, or things — with little or no connection to them.

Think of an island in the middle of the ocean. Nothing connects it to the mainland. No bridge, no road, no easy path. That physical picture — something cut off, standing alone, disconnected — is the perfect image of isolation.

The key ingredients are always the same: separation and lack of connection.

Isolation is a rich word. It is used in everyday life, in science, in medicine, in politics, and in emotional conversations. But the central idea stays the same in all of them — something is cut off from the rest.

1. Social and Personal Isolation

This is the most common use. When a person is isolated, they are cut off from other people. They have little or no contact with friends, family, or the wider community.

This can happen in two ways:

  • Forced isolation — something outside your control separates you. For example, a person who moves to a remote village where they know no one, or a prisoner kept alone in a cell, is experiencing forced isolation. They didn't choose it.
  • Chosen isolation — sometimes a person deliberately withdraws from others. A writer who locks themselves in a cabin in the woods for a month to finish a book is choosing isolation. Here, it is voluntary and purposeful.

Notice that isolation doesn't always mean you are physically alone. A person can be surrounded by hundreds of people and still be in isolation — if they have no meaningful connection to any of them. A new student at a school where everyone already knows each other can feel completely isolated even in a crowded hallway.

2. Emotional Isolation

This refers to a feeling — the inner experience of being alone, misunderstood, or disconnected, even when others are present. A person going through grief, depression, or trauma often describes a deep sense of isolation — as if a glass wall separates them from the rest of the world. People are physically near, but emotionally, they feel entirely alone.

3. Medical Isolation

In medicine and public health, isolation means keeping a sick person deliberately separated from healthy people to stop a disease from spreading. During a contagious illness, a patient may be placed in an isolation ward — a section of the hospital where contact with others is strictly controlled.

It is also used the other way around. If a person has a very weak immune system, they might be isolated from germs and the outside world to protect them, rather than to protect others.

4. Scientific Isolation

Scientists isolate things all the time. If a chemist wants to study one specific substance, they separate it from everything else — purify it, extract it, remove all other variables. That process is called isolation. Similarly, in biology, you might isolate a single gene or a single bacteria cell to examine it closely. The idea is the same: remove it from everything else so you can study it on its own terms.

5. Political and Economic Isolation

Countries can be isolated too. When the rest of the world refuses to trade with, communicate with, or maintain diplomatic relations with a particular country, that country is in a state of political or economic isolation. It is cut off from the global community. This can be a punishment (called sanctions), or it can happen because a country's government chooses to close itself off.
Isolation Can Be Positive or Negative

This is important: isolation is not always a bad thing.

When it is negative: Prolonged social isolation is seriously harmful to human beings. Humans are social creatures, and when cut off from meaningful connection for a long time, people suffer mentally and physically. Loneliness, depression, anxiety, and even physical health problems can result from long-term isolation.

When it is positive or neutral: A scientist isolating a compound is doing something precise and useful. A person choosing to spend a weekend in isolation to rest, reflect, or create is doing something healthy and intentional. A patient in medical isolation is being kept safe (or keeping others safe). In these cases, isolation is a tool, not a punishment.

The same word, the same concept — but the meaning shifts depending on context and intent.

Isolation is not always total or complete. It exists on a spectrum.

  • Complete isolation means zero contact or connection — a prisoner in solitary confinement, or a scientist working in a completely sterile, sealed environment.
  • Partial isolation means reduced contact — a person who rarely leaves home, has very few friends, and avoids social situations is partially isolated.

You will often see words like relative isolation, near-isolation, or increasing isolation to show that isolation is not always all-or-nothing.

• In isolation — This phrase means "on its own," "without context," or "separately." For example: "If you look at that one sentence in isolation, it sounds rude — but in context, it was perfectly kind." Here, isolation means you are examining something without considering its surroundings or connections.
  • Isolation from — Used to describe what someone or something is cut off from. "Her isolation from her family was painful."
  • Sense of isolation / feeling of isolation — Used to describe the emotional experience of being disconnected.
  • Isolation ward — A section of a hospital for patients with contagious diseases.
  • Social isolation — Being cut off from social contact and community.
  • Self-isolation — Deliberately isolating yourself, often used in a medical context (staying home when you might be sick).
How Isolation Differs from Similar Words

Two words are often confused with isolation: solitude and loneliness.

  • Solitude is being alone, but it tends to carry a peaceful, chosen, even pleasant feeling. A poet who loves to write in solitude is happy being alone.
  • Loneliness is an emotion — the painful feeling of wanting connection but not having it. You can be lonely in a crowd.
  • Isolation is more about the state or condition of being separated or disconnected — it is more objective and structural. But it can certainly cause loneliness.

Think of it this way: isolation describes the situation, loneliness describes the feeling that often comes from that situation, and solitude is being alone by choice, usually peacefully.
One Sentence to Remember It By

Isolation is the state of being cut off — from people, from society, from connection, or from other substances — so that interaction or contact is absent or severely limited.

Everything else builds from that.
9352:
Isolationism is a country's deliberate policy of staying out of the affairs of other countries — their wars, their conflicts, their alliances, and their political disagreements — and instead focusing almost entirely on what is happening within its own borders.

Think of it like a neighbor who refuses to get involved in anyone else's arguments on the street, never joins a neighborhood watch group, never lends tools or borrows them, and simply keeps to themselves behind a closed gate. That neighbor is practicing a kind of isolationism.
What It Actually Means in Practice

When a country adopts isolationism, it typically does one or more of the following:

It refuses to join military alliances, meaning it won't agree to defend other countries or ask them to defend it. It avoids sending its soldiers to fight in foreign wars, even when terrible things are happening in other parts of the world. It pulls back from international organizations that require member countries to cooperate, follow shared rules, or contribute money and resources. It reduces or eliminates trade with other nations (this economic side is sometimes called protectionism, but it often goes hand-in-hand with isolationism). It declines to sign international treaties that would bind it to global commitments.

The underlying logic is simple: our country's problems come first, and getting involved abroad only brings us trouble, cost, and risk.

Countries don't embrace isolationism randomly. There are usually clear reasons driving it.

A desire for self-preservation. A country may believe that getting entangled in foreign wars will drain its wealth, cost lives, and create enemies it wouldn't otherwise have. If you don't pick sides, the thinking goes, no one has a reason to attack you.

A belief in self-sufficiency. Some countries feel they have enough resources, land, and people to thrive without depending on the outside world. Why rely on others when you can stand on your own feet?

Distrust of the outside world. Past experiences of being exploited, colonized, or manipulated by foreign powers can make a country deeply suspicious of international entanglements.

A focus on internal problems. Leaders may argue that poverty, inequality, infrastructure, or social issues at home deserve full attention rather than money and energy spent abroad.

A strong sense of national identity. Some nations believe their culture, values, or way of life is best protected by limiting foreign influence.

Isolationism is not always all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum.

Hard isolationism is extreme and rare. A country completely seals itself off from the world — no trade, no diplomacy, no contact. North Korea today is perhaps the closest modern example. Japan practiced something similar between the 17th and 19th centuries under a policy called Sakoku, during which foreigners were banned and Japanese citizens were forbidden from leaving.

Soft isolationism is far more common. A country still trades and communicates with others, but it deliberately avoids military commitments, foreign wars, and international political organizations. It participates in the world economy but refuses to be the world's police officer or partner in collective security arrangements.
The Most Famous Historical Example: The United States

The United States is the country most associated with isolationism in modern history, particularly before World War II.

After World War I ended in 1918, many Americans were exhausted and disillusioned. Tens of millions had died in that war, and many Americans felt the U.S. had no business getting involved in Europe's endless conflicts. The U.S. Senate even refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles or allow the country to join the League of Nations — an international peacekeeping body — because joining would have obligated the U.S. to get involved in future foreign disputes.

Throughout the 1930s, as Adolf Hitler rose to power in Germany and war clouds gathered over Europe and Asia, a powerful isolationist movement in America insisted the country should stay out of it. Organizations like the America First Committee drew massive public support. It was only the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 — a direct attack on American soil — that ended this period of isolationism and pulled the U.S. into World War II.

After the war, the U.S. largely abandoned isolationism and became deeply involved in global affairs, forming alliances like NATO and engaging militarily and diplomatically around the world.
Don't Confuse It With These Related Concepts

Neutrality is not the same as isolationism. A neutral country — like Switzerland — may be deeply connected to the world through trade, diplomacy, and international organizations, but simply refuses to take sides in wars. An isolationist country tries to avoid international engagement more broadly.

Non-interventionism is a narrower version of the idea. A non-interventionist country stays out of other nations' internal affairs and wars but may still trade freely, maintain diplomatic relationships, and participate in international institutions. Think of it as isolationism's more moderate cousin.

Protectionism refers only to economic policy — raising tariffs and barriers to protect domestic industries from foreign competition. A country can be economically protectionist without being politically or militarily isolationist.

Isolationism has genuine, respectable arguments behind it — it is not simply foolishness.

It saves lives and money. A country that doesn't fight foreign wars doesn't send its young people home in coffins or spend trillions on military campaigns. It preserves sovereignty. When a country joins alliances and international bodies, it gives up some control over its own decisions. Isolationism preserves full self-governance. It can prevent unnecessary enemies. Intervening in foreign conflicts often creates resentment, blowback, and new enemies. Standing back can mean fewer people want to hurt you.

Critics of isolationism argue it is naive and ultimately self-defeating in the modern world.

The world is deeply interconnected. Global trade, the internet, pandemics, climate change, terrorism, and financial systems mean that what happens far away inevitably affects you — whether you want it to or not. Isolationism doesn't make these problems go away; it just means you face them without allies or influence. It can also embolden aggressors. When powerful countries withdraw from international affairs, it can create a vacuum that dangerous actors fill. Many historians argue that American isolationism in the 1930s gave Hitler room to expand before anyone stopped him. Finally, it can harm a country's economy. Cutting off from global trade and investment usually makes a country poorer, not richer.

Isolationism resurfaces as a live political debate in many countries whenever people feel that international commitments have become too costly or unfair. Movements like "America First" in the United States, Brexit in the United Kingdom, and various nationalist movements across Europe all carry elements of isolationist thinking — a desire to pull back, protect national interests, and disengage from the burdens of global leadership.

Understanding isolationism helps you make sense of major debates in the news about trade wars, military alliances, immigration, and international cooperation — because underneath many of these arguments is the same fundamental tension: Should we engage with the world, or protect ourselves from it?

In short, isolationism is a country's conscious choice to turn inward, keep to itself, and stay out of the world's affairs — driven by the belief that national security, prosperity, and identity are best protected not by engaging with the world, but by keeping a safe distance from it.
9353:
An isolationist is a person who believes that their country should stay out of the business of other countries — their wars, their politics, their conflicts — and instead focus all of its energy inward, on its own people and its own problems.

Think of it this way: imagine you live in a neighborhood and there are constant arguments, fights, and disputes between your neighbors. An isolationist is like the person who says, "This is not my problem. I'm going to close my door, tend to my own house, and not get involved."

An isolationist holds the view that their nation's best interests are served by minimizing or avoiding involvement in international affairs. This typically means opposing:

  • Sending soldiers to fight in foreign wars
  • Forming military alliances with other nations
  • Stationing troops or military bases in other countries
  • Getting entangled in other nations' conflicts, even diplomatically

The central argument of an isolationist is simple: "We have enough problems at home. Why spend our money, our soldiers' lives, and our political energy on the affairs of countries far away?"

This is important to understand clearly.

An isolationist is not someone who is personally shy, withdrawn, or anti-social. That would be an introvert. The word "isolationist" is purely about a nation's relationship with the outside world — it is a political and foreign policy term.

Also, being an isolationist doesn't necessarily mean wanting to cut off all contact with the world. Most isolationists are perfectly fine with trade, tourism, and cultural exchange. What they resist is political and military entanglement — being dragged into other countries' quarrels, wars, or power games.

Not all isolationists think exactly the same way. There is a spectrum.

On one end, you have hard isolationists, who want their country to withdraw from virtually everything international — no alliances, no foreign aid, no involvement whatsoever. Think of it as building a very tall wall around the country in every political and military sense.

On the other end, you have soft isolationists, who are simply very cautious and restrained about foreign involvement. They don't want to be the world's police force. They'll pick their moments carefully and only act when their nation's direct interests are clearly at stake.

To understand a word fully, it helps to know its opposite.

The opposite of an isolationist is an interventionist — someone who believes their country should actively involve itself in world affairs, sometimes even proactively. Interventionists might argue that it's their nation's duty, or in their nation's strategic interest, to go abroad, form alliances, fight in conflicts, and shape global events.

There is also the internationalist, who believes nations should cooperate together through international organizations and treaties to solve global problems collectively.

An isolationist would look at both of these and say: "You're getting us into trouble that isn't ours."

The word "isolationist" is most commonly used in discussions of foreign policy — the set of decisions a government makes about how to deal with other countries.

You'll often hear it used in sentences like:

  • "The senator is a well-known isolationist who has consistently voted against sending troops abroad."
  • "His foreign policy is essentially isolationist — he believes America should come first, always."
  • "Critics called her an isolationist, but she preferred the term 'non-interventionist.'"

Notice that last example. This brings up a subtle but important point: "isolationist" is sometimes used as a criticism, implying that the person is naïve, selfish, or short-sighted about the realities of the world. Because of this negative connotation, many people who hold isolationist views prefer to call themselves things like "non-interventionist," "restraint advocate," or simply someone who believes in "putting the country first." The substance of the belief is often the same; it's just the label they resist.

The United States is the most famous historical example to understand this word.

Before the US entered World War II, there was a powerful isolationist movement in America. Many Americans felt strongly that Europe's war was Europe's problem, and the US should stay home. A major political group called the America First Committee rallied around this isolationist position, arguing that America had nothing to gain by entering the conflict. After the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, public opinion flipped rapidly and the US entered the war — and the isolationist movement essentially collapsed.

This example shows the core tension: isolationists argue that staying out protects the nation; their critics argue that the world is too interconnected for any country to truly stand apart, and that inaction has its own consequences.

If you had to capture the whole word in one sentence:

An isolationist is a person who believes their country should mind its own business — staying out of foreign wars, refusing to be bound by international alliances, and focusing its resources on domestic affairs rather than getting entangled in the rest of the world's problems.
9354:
An isotope is one of two or more forms of the same chemical element, where each form has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in its nucleus.

To fully grasp this, you need a quick refresher on atomic structure.
The Building Blocks: A Quick Recap

Every atom has a tiny, dense center called the nucleus, surrounded by electrons. The nucleus is made of two types of particles:

  • Protons — positively charged particles. The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number, and this number is what defines which element it is. All carbon atoms have 6 protons. All oxygen atoms have 8. This never changes for a given element.
  • Neutrons — particles with no charge. They sit alongside protons in the nucleus and add to the atom's mass, but they do not change what element it is.

The total count of protons plus neutrons is called the mass number.
So What Exactly Is an Isotope?

Since the number of protons must stay fixed for an element to remain that element, the only thing that can vary between atoms of the same element is the number of neutrons. When two atoms belong to the same element but have different neutron counts, they are called isotopes of each other.

Think of isotopes as different "versions" of the same element — same identity (same protons), different weight (different neutrons).
A Clear Example: The Isotopes of Carbon

Carbon always has 6 protons. But it exists in three naturally occurring isotopes:

Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons → mass number = 12
Carbon-13 has 6 protons and 7 neutrons → mass number = 13
Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons → mass number = 14

All three are undeniably carbon — they behave nearly identically in chemical reactions and can form the same bonds. But they differ in mass, and this difference has enormous practical consequences (more on that shortly).

The naming convention is simple: you write the element's name (or symbol) followed by the mass number. So Carbon-14 is also written as ¹⁴C.

Not all isotopes are created equal. Some are stable — their nuclei hold together indefinitely and do not change. Carbon-12 and Carbon-13 are stable isotopes.

Others are unstable, meaning their nuclei are not in a balanced, comfortable state. Over time, they spontaneously break down and emit energy or particles in a process called radioactive decay. These are called radioactive isotopes (also called radioisotopes). Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope.

What makes a nucleus unstable? Generally, having too many or too few neutrons relative to the protons upsets the balance of forces inside the nucleus, making it prone to decay. The larger the imbalance, the faster it decays.

Every radioactive isotope has a characteristic half-life — the time it takes for half of a given sample of that isotope to decay into something else. Half-lives range from fractions of a second (for highly unstable isotopes) to billions of years (for mildly unstable ones). Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.

Most elements in nature don't exist as a single pure isotope — they exist as a natural mixture of isotopes, each present in a characteristic proportion. For example, about 98.9% of all carbon on Earth is Carbon-12, about 1.1% is Carbon-13, and Carbon-14 exists only in trace amounts.

This is why the atomic weight you see on a periodic table is not a whole number. For carbon, it's approximately 12.011 — a weighted average reflecting the natural mixture of its isotopes.

The differences between isotopes, though subtle, have profound real-world consequences.

Radiocarbon dating is one of the most famous applications. Living organisms constantly absorb Carbon-14 from the atmosphere. When an organism dies, it stops absorbing it, and the Carbon-14 already inside begins to decay at a known, steady rate. By measuring how much Carbon-14 remains in an ancient artifact or fossil, scientists can calculate how long ago it died — often with remarkable precision, going back up to about 50,000 years.

Nuclear energy and weapons rely on isotopes of uranium. Uranium-235 is fissile — its nucleus can be split to release enormous energy. Uranium-238 is far more abundant but much harder to split. Enriching uranium means increasing the proportion of U-235 relative to U-238.

Medical imaging and cancer treatment use radioactive isotopes extensively. Technetium-99m (a radioactive isotope of technetium) is injected into patients and emits radiation that scanners can detect, creating images of organs. Iodine-131 is used to destroy cancerous thyroid tissue because the thyroid naturally absorbs iodine, concentrating the radioactive isotope exactly where it's needed.

Scientific research uses stable isotopes as tracers. By replacing a common isotope in a molecule with a heavier one (say, swapping ordinary hydrogen for deuterium, which is hydrogen with one extra neutron), scientists can track exactly how that molecule moves and transforms inside a living body or a chemical reaction — without introducing any radioactivity.

An isotope is a variant of an element defined by its unique neutron count. Same element, same protons, different neutrons, different mass. Isotopes can be stable or radioactive. They are not exotic laboratory curiosities — they exist naturally all around us, inside us, and are essential tools in medicine, energy, archaeology, and science.
9355:
Issuance means the act of officially putting something out into the world — releasing it, distributing it, or making it formally available to people.

Think of it this way: when an authority, organisation, or official body creates something and then sends it out or hands it out in a formal, deliberate way, that entire process is called issuance.

The word comes from the verb "to issue", which means to officially put something out. Issuance is simply the noun form — it names the act of doing that.
The Two Key Features of Issuance

To truly understand the word, keep these two things in mind:

1. It is always formal or official.
Issuance doesn't describe casual giving or sharing. It describes a structured, deliberate act — usually done by an authority (a government, a bank, a court, an organisation). You wouldn't use "issuance" to describe a friend giving you a book.

2. It refers to the act, not the thing itself.
Issuance is the process of putting something out — not the document, product, or item that was put out. For example, "the issuance of a passport" means the act of creating and giving out the passport, not the passport itself.

The word appears most often in formal, legal, financial, and governmental contexts. Here are the main areas:

Government & Legal
Governments and courts issue official documents and orders. The act of doing so is "issuance."

  • The issuance of a visa can take several weeks.
  • The issuance of the court order immediately halted the project.
  • The issuance of a search warrant requires a judge's approval.

Finance & Business
Companies and governments issue stocks, bonds, currency, and shares to raise money or put them into circulation.

  • The issuance of new shares allowed the company to raise funds.
  • The central bank was responsible for the issuance of the new currency.
  • Investors were excited about the issuance of government bonds.

Statements & Reports
Organisations and officials formally "issue" statements, warnings, guidelines, and reports. The act is called "issuance."

  • The issuance of a public health warning came too late.
  • The issuance of new safety guidelines changed how the factory operated.
  • The issuance of the annual report is expected next Monday.

Licences & Certificates
Any time an authority formally hands out permits, licences, or certificates, that act is called issuance.

  • The issuance of a driving licence requires passing a test.
  • The issuance of building permits was delayed due to new regulations.

These two words are closely linked and easy to confuse, so it helps to be clear:

  • Issue (verb) = the action → "The government will issue new passports."
  • Issuance (noun) = the name of that action → "The issuance of new passports will begin next month."

They describe the same event — issuance just packages the idea as a thing you can talk about, rather than an action happening in a sentence.

The "issuer" — the one performing the issuance — is almost always a body with some kind of authority or power:

  • A government (issuance of IDs, passports, laws, notices)
  • A court (issuance of warrants, injunctions, judgements)
  • A company or bank (issuance of stocks, bonds, credit cards)
  • An organisation (issuance of reports, statements, guidelines)
  • A school or institution (issuance of certificates, degrees)

This is why "issuance" always feels formal — the authority behind it is baked into the word itself.

Certain words appear beside "issuance" very frequently. Recognising these combinations will help you use the word naturally:

  • The issuance of + [something] — this is the most common structure. "The issuance of a licence."
  • Prior to issuance — before the official release of something.
  • Upon issuance — at the moment something is officially released. "The contract takes effect upon issuance."
  • Pending issuance — while waiting for something to be officially issued.
  • Issuance date — the official date on which something was issued.
  • Issuance of debt / bonds / shares — very common in finance and banking.

It helps to know what the word doesn't mean:

  • It is not the same as simply giving or lending something — those are informal acts. Issuance is always official.
  • It is not the thing that was issued — just the act of issuing it.
  • It does not imply permanence necessarily — something can be issued and later cancelled or revoked. The issuance itself is just the moment of official release.

Issuance = the formal, official act of putting something out — whether it's a document, a financial instrument, a statement, or an order — typically done by a person or body with authority.

Once you remember that "issuance" always means an official act of releasing or putting something out, you will recognise it instantly in any context — legal, financial, governmental, or otherwise — and use it with complete confidence.
9356: "Issue" has several distinct meanings. Each one matters, and you'll encounter all of them.

(The most common everyday meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use the word today. An "issue" is something that is wrong, not working, or causing trouble.

  • "There's an issue with the internet connection."
  • "She's dealing with some personal issues."
  • "The mechanic found an issue with the brakes."

Important nuance: "Issue" is deliberately softer than "problem." Saying "there's an issue" sounds more manageable and less alarming than "there's a problem." This is why you hear it so often in professional settings — people use it to signal concern without causing panic.
2. An Important Topic, Especially One People Disagree About

An "issue" can also be a subject that people care about, discuss, or argue over — particularly in society, politics, or public life.

  • "Climate change is one of the biggest issues of our time."
  • "The candidates discussed several key issues."
  • "This is a sensitive issue that affects millions of families."

Here, an issue isn't a personal problem — it's a matter of collective concern. It might not have one clear answer, and reasonable people may hold different views on it.
3. A Single Edition of a Publication

When talking about magazines, newspapers, academic journals, or newsletters, "issue" refers to one specific published edition — one copy released at a particular point in time.

  • "Have you read the latest issue of National Geographic?"
  • "The January issue had a fascinating cover story."
  • "This study appeared in the March issue of the journal."

A magazine publishes many times throughout the year. Each individually released version is one issue. So you can speak of the "April issue," the "winter issue," or "issue number 23."
4. The Official Release or Distribution of Something

In formal and official contexts, "issue" refers to the act of officially putting something out — and also to the things that are given out through that act.

  • "The government announced the issue of new identity cards."
  • "The post office released a special commemorative issue of stamps."
  • "The company raised money through a public share issue." (releasing shares for people to buy)
  • "Soldiers received a standard issue uniform." (the uniform officially given to all soldiers — nothing special or personalised)

When something is called "standard issue," it means it's the standard, official version routinely given out — not customised.

This is an older meaning, mostly found in legal documents, wills, and formal literature. In this sense, "issue" means a person's children or direct blood descendants.

  • "He died without issue." — He died without having any children.
  • "The property is to be divided equally among his issue." — Among his children.
  • "If she dies without issue, the estate passes to her siblings."

You will almost never use this meaning in everyday speech, but you'll encounter it in legal writing, old novels, historical documents, and formal contexts.

In older or very formal writing, "issue" can mean the final result of something — how a situation turned out.

  • "The issue of the battle was still uncertain." — The outcome.
  • "They waited for the issue of the peace talks."

This meaning is rare in modern everyday language, but you may come across it in older texts.

"At issue"
Something is "at issue" when it is the specific matter being questioned or disputed.

  • "The contract exists — what is at issue is who must pay first."
  • "The point at issue is whether he was given prior permission."

"Take issue with"
To "take issue with" something means to disagree with it or challenge it.

  • "I take issue with your conclusion — the data doesn't support it."
  • "She took issue with the way the report described events."

"Make an issue of"
To "make an issue of" something means to treat it as a serious problem worthy of attention, especially when others would rather move on.

  • "I don't want to make an issue of it, but I feel I was treated unfairly."
  • "He made an issue out of a very minor mistake."

"The issue at hand"
The specific matter that is currently being dealt with or discussed right now.

  • "Let's stay focused on the issue at hand."

"A side issue"
A matter related to the main topic but less important than the central concern.

  • "The question of timing is a side issue — let's address the core problem first."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

The context will almost always make it obvious:

  • Casual conversation about something going wrong → a problem (Meaning 1)
  • News, politics, social life → a topic of debate (Meaning 2)
  • Magazines, journals, newspapers → an edition (Meaning 3)
  • Governments, institutions, official acts → official release (Meaning 4)
  • Legal documents, old literature → children/descendants (Meaning 5)
  • Old or formal writing about events → outcome (Meaning 6)
The One Thread Running Through All Meanings

If you look at all six meanings together, you'll notice something: every sense of "issue" involves something coming out or being put forward — a problem that surfaces, a topic that comes up for debate, an edition that comes out, something officially released, offspring that come from a person, a result that comes out of a situation. Noticing this can help you intuitively understand any new use of the word you encounter in the future, even in an unfamiliar context.
9357:
When something is issued, it is formally and officially sent out, given out, or put out — usually by a person or organization that has the authority to do so.

Think of it this way: "issue" is not just giving something. It is giving something in an official, deliberate way, from a position of authority.
The Main Meaning — To Officially Send or Give Out

This is the most common and important meaning of the verb "issue."

When a government, organization, court, company, or official body formally produces and sends something out to the public or to specific people, they issue it.

Examples:

  • The government issued new passports to citizens.
  • The police issued a warning to the public.
  • The judge issued an arrest warrant.
  • The company issued a press statement after the accident.
  • The bank issued her a credit card.
  • The school issued certificates to all graduating students.
  • The doctor issued a prescription.

In every one of these examples, notice the pattern:

An authority → officially produces/sends something → to a recipient

The "something" being issued is always a real, concrete thing — a document, a warning, an order, a card, a statement. It is not vague. It is not casual. It carries the weight of officialdom.

This is crucial to understand, because "issue" is often confused with simpler words.

"Give" is a general, everyday word. Anyone can give anything to anyone.

She gave her friend a book.

"Issue" is formal and official. It implies that the giver has authority, that the action is deliberate and documented, and that the thing being sent out usually has official status or consequences.

The court issued a subpoena.

You would never say "The court gave a subpoena." That sounds too casual and strips away the legal weight of the action. "Issue" carries the formality that the situation demands.

Similarly, you could technically say "The government sent out new passports," but "issued" is the precise, professional word because it communicates that this was an official, authorized act — not a casual sending.

The short rule:

When something official is formally put out by an authority, use issue, not just "give" or "send."

The verb "issue" is almost always followed by a specific type of thing. Here are the main categories:

Official documents:
passports, visas, licenses, permits, certificates, tickets, warrants, summons, deeds

Official communications:
statements, warnings, notices, alerts, directives, orders, decrees, ultimatums, apologies (formal ones), guidelines

Financial instruments:
shares, stocks, bonds, currency, checks, credit cards, invoices, refunds

Publications:
reports, editions of a magazine or journal (e.g., "They issued a new report on climate change.")

"Issue" follows a few natural patterns:

Pattern 1: [Subject] issued [something]

The WHO issued a global health alert.

Pattern 2: [Subject] issued [something] to [someone]

The embassy issued a visa to the applicant.

Pattern 3: [Something] was issued by [Subject] (passive voice)

A statement was issued by the company's CEO.
Arrest warrants were issued by the judge.

The passive voice is extremely common with "issue" because official communications are often talked about in terms of what was produced, not who produced it. You will see this frequently in news writing.
The Second Meaning — To Flow or Come Out of Something

This is a less common but important meaning, used in formal, literary, or descriptive writing.

When something issues from a place, it flows out of it or emerges from it.

Examples:

  • Thick smoke issued from the burning building.
  • A strange sound issued from behind the closed door.
  • Blood issued from the wound.
  • A long sigh issued from her lips.

Here, "issue" paints a picture of something coming out of a source, almost like a stream or flow. You are unlikely to hear this in everyday conversation — it belongs to formal writing, journalism, or literature. But you will encounter it, so it is important to recognize it.
The Third Meaning — To Come from or Result from

In very formal writing, "issue from" can also mean to arise from or to stem from — that is, something originates or results from a cause.

Examples:

  • Many of society's problems issue from poverty and inequality.
  • The conflict issued from decades of misunderstanding.

This meaning is rare in modern everyday English, but it appears in academic and formal texts. The idea is the same as the "flow out" sense — something comes out of a source, but here the source is a cause, not a physical place.

"Issue" is a formal word. It belongs to the language of governments, legal systems, corporations, institutions, and journalism.

You would say:

The court issued a ruling. ✅

You would not casually say:

"I'll issue you a slice of cake." ❌ — This sounds strange and overly stiff.

Stick to using "issue" in contexts that involve official acts, organizations, formal documents, or authoritative actions. In casual conversation, "give," "send," or "hand out" are more natural.

Primary meaningTo officially and formally send out, give out, or put out something — by an authority
Secondary meaningTo flow or come out of a source (formal/literary)
Tertiary meaningTo arise or result from a cause (very formal)
RegisterFormal — used in law, government, business, journalism
Key question to askIs an authority formally putting something out? → Use "issue"

The single most important thing to hold onto: "issue" is about official, authorized putting-out. Whenever a body with power formally produces and sends something into the world — a document, a statement, a warning — that is the verb at work.
9358:
An isthmus is a narrow strip of land that connects two larger landmasses, with water running along both of its sides.

Think of a dumbbell: two heavy weights on either end, joined by a thin handle in the middle. The handle is the isthmus. The two weights are the larger landmasses. The space around everything is water.

For something to qualify as an isthmus, four things must be true: it is made of land, it is notably narrow compared to what it connects, it links two larger landmasses, and it has water along both of its long sides.
Picture the letter H. The two tall vertical bars are two large landmasses. The short horizontal bar connecting them in the middle — that is the isthmus. Water fills everything around it.

The Isthmus of Panama is the most famous in the world. It is the thin strip of land connecting North America to South America, with the Pacific Ocean on one side and the Caribbean Sea on the other. Because this strip is so narrow, humans cut a canal right through it — the Panama Canal — so that ships could pass between the two oceans without sailing all the way around the bottom of South America.

The Isthmus of Suez connects Africa to Asia, with the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the Red Sea to the south. Again, because of this narrow land connection, the Suez Canal was built here, saving ships thousands of miles of travel around the entire continent of Africa.

The Isthmus of Corinth in Greece connects the Greek mainland to the Peloponnese region, with the Ionian Sea on one side and the Aegean Sea on the other. A canal was built here too, for the same reason.

Notice a pattern? Canals are almost always built through isthmuses, because an isthmus is the thinnest point of land between two bodies of water — the most logical place to dig through.

Since an isthmus is often the only land route between two large regions, whoever controls it controls the flow of people, armies, and trade between those regions. This has made isthmuses some of the most fought-over and economically critical pieces of land in history. Even today, the Panama and Suez Canals — both built through isthmuses — are among the most important shipping routes on Earth.

Beyond geography, "isthmus" is also used in medicine and biology to describe a narrow connecting section between two larger parts of an organ — because the shape is identical to the geographic idea.

For example, the thyroid gland in your neck has two large lobes, one on each side of your throat, joined together by a thin band of tissue in the middle. That connecting band is called the isthmus of the thyroid. It is named exactly the same way a geographic isthmus is — a narrow connector between two larger parts.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are easy to mix up with isthmus, so it helps to see how they differ:

Peninsula — Land that is surrounded by water on three sides, but attached to a larger landmass on one side. A peninsula only connects to one landmass; it doesn't bridge two. Florida, for instance, is a peninsula. An isthmus, by contrast, always connects two larger landmasses.

Strait — Think of a strait as the water version of an isthmus. A strait is a narrow passage of water connecting two larger bodies of water, with land on either side. The Strait of Gibraltar, for example, is the narrow strip of water between Europe and Africa connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea. An isthmus and a strait are essentially mirror images of each other — one is a narrow land bridge with water on the sides, the other is a narrow water channel with land on the sides.

Cape — A cape is simply a pointed or rounded piece of land that juts out into a body of water. It does not connect anything to anything else.
The standard plural is isthmuses. You may sometimes also see the Latin plural isthmi, but "isthmuses" is the correct and widely accepted form in modern English.

An isthmus is a narrow land connector between two larger landmasses, flanked by water on both long sides. It can refer to geography (land bridges between continents or regions) or anatomy (narrow tissue bridges between parts of an organ). Its defining characteristic is always the same: narrow, connecting, flanked by something larger on each end.
9359:
"It goes without saying" means that something is so obvious, so well-known, or so universally understood that there is no real need to say it out loud — yet you are saying it anyway, usually to stress its importance or to be clear.

Think of it this way: if you invited a friend to dinner, you wouldn't normally say "please don't bring a tiger." Why? Because it goes without saying. Everyone already knows that. No one needs to be told.

The word "goes" here doesn't mean movement. It means "exists" or "holds true." Think of phrases like "anything goes" (anything is acceptable) or "as the saying goes" (as the common expression exists). So "it goes without saying" literally means: this truth exists even without being spoken.

Here is the beautiful, clever twist in this idiom: you always say it right before saying the very thing you claim doesn't need to be said.

"It goes without saying that you should be honest in a job interview."

You said it. You literally just said the thing that "goes without saying." This is intentional. The speaker uses the phrase to:

  • Acknowledge that the point seems obvious.
  • But still make the point — because it's important enough to reinforce.

So the idiom is a polite, smart way of saying: "I know you probably already know this, but let me say it clearly anyway."
How It Is Used in Sentences

The phrase almost always appears at the beginning of a sentence, followed by "that" and the obvious point:

  • "It goes without saying that hard work leads to success."
  • "It goes without saying that you should respect your elders."
  • "It goes without saying that safety comes first."

You can also use it after making a point, as a comment:

  • "You must wear a seatbelt — that goes without saying."

Notice that in this second structure, we use "that goes without saying" (with "that" replacing "it," referring back to the point just made).

This idiom carries a calm, confident, slightly formal tone. It signals that the speaker is reasonable and not trying to be condescending — they are simply reinforcing something important. It works well in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Formal writing
  • Speeches and presentations
  • Professional emails

It is not sarcastic by nature, though it can be used sarcastically in casual speech (e.g., "It goes without saying that he forgot the keys… again.")

Do not confuse it with:

  • "It is said that..." → This means something is rumored or claimed by others. Completely different.
  • "Needless to say" → This is a near-perfect synonym (see below), but "it goes without saying" sounds slightly more formal and measured.
  • "Obviously" → While similar in meaning, just saying "obviously" can sometimes sound rude or dismissive. "It goes without saying" is gentler and more conversational.

These phrases mean almost the same thing and can often replace each other:

  • "Needless to say" — the most common and closest substitute.
    "Needless to say, he was thrilled with the news."*
  • "Of course" — more casual and shorter.
    "Of course, you should always back up your files."*
  • "Obviously" — direct, but can sometimes feel blunt or condescending depending on the tone.
  • "As everyone knows" — slightly more formal.

Among all of these, "it goes without saying" and "needless to say" are the most interchangeable.

The phrase is a translation of the French expression "cela va sans dire", which means exactly the same thing — "that goes without saying." It entered the English language in the 19th century and became widely used. Over time, it became a standard idiom in English, completely detached from its French roots.

Mistake 1: Using it for things that are NOT actually obvious.
The whole point of the idiom is that the thing seems universally understood. If you say "It goes without saying that the meeting is on Tuesday" — that's wrong usage, because people genuinely might not know when the meeting is. Use it only for things that are broadly understood or logically apparent.

Mistake 2: Overusing it.
If you use it in every other sentence, it loses its effect. Reserve it for moments when you truly want to signal: "this is so fundamental, it almost doesn't need to be stated."

Mistake 3: Confusing the two structures.

  • ✅ It goes without saying that you should be kind.
  • ✅ That goes without saying. (used after you've already made the point)
  • ❌ This goes without saying that... — this is grammatically incorrect.

MeaningSomething is so obvious it almost doesn't need to be stated — but you're stating it anyway for emphasis or clarity.
Structure"It goes without saying that [obvious point]." OR "[Point] — that goes without saying."
ToneCalm, confident, polite, slightly formal
Closest synonym"Needless to say"
OriginFrench — cela va sans dire (19th century)

It goes without saying that once you truly understand an idiom — its meaning, its structure, its tone, and its traps — you can use it with full confidence. And now, you do.
